agent-instructions.md#ai-rulez-is-the-op.text:
`include_ai_rulez` (default off, `full` preset) with an `ai_rulez_presets`
multiselect renders `.ai-rulez/` sources from which ai-rulez generates each
host's native instruction files and skill copies. With the toggle off, the
hand-written `AGENTS.md` and the Claude-only skills render. The section prose
lives once in `_macros.jinja`; both the hand-written file and the rule sources
call the same macros. The pin lives in its own `agents` dependency group,
exact, Renovate-tracked through the native uv manager.

**Reason:** the generated project's branch-name check already whitelists five
agent prefixes, but only Claude received the repo-setup skill and only two
hosts received instructions; hand-writing five formats is the duplication the
template exists to remove. ai-rulez ships on PyPI (no Node) and has the cobo
shape — sources in, committed output out, a check that proves they agree. A
second hand-maintained copy of the paragraphs would recreate inside the
template the drift it removes downstream. Its own group because `dev` includes
`style` wholesale and only two callers invoke the tool; upstream's pre-commit
hooks would add a second `rev` pin. The exact pin matters because the PyPI
launcher downloads a Go binary and proceeds with a warning if the checksum file
cannot be fetched.

**Rejected alternative:** hand-written per-host files — five dialects drifting.

agent-instructions.md#generated-host-fil.text:
The template renders `.ai-rulez/` and stops. `AGENTS.md`, the Copilot
instructions and the per-host skill copies are written by the adopter's first
`ai-rulez generate` and committed from then on. Turning the toggle on via
update leaves a project with no instruction files until the generator runs
(the after-update message names the two commands; CI is red until the output
is committed). Turning it off requires running ai-rulez's clean command before
the update, while the sources it reads still exist, because the host files are
not copier-managed and would otherwise stay committed and stale.

**Reason:** copier's renderer and ai-rulez's renderer produce different bytes
for the same content (ai-rulez composes its own headings and stamps a
provenance header with a content hash), so rendering both would diff on first
generate and every `copier update` would re-render on top of generated files —
churn on files the adopter never touched. As build output they sit outside the
3-way merge, which then covers only the small per-rule sources. Neither
direction is automatic because the template has no tasks. Dropping the toggle
from `full` was rejected: `full` means every toggle, and a preset that quietly
omits one is a worse surprise than a loud one.

**Rejected alternative:** render the generated files as well — the churn above.

agent-instructions.md#no-builtin-ai-rule.text:
`builtins = false`: the shipped rules are only the project's own.
`gitignore = false`: the generated output is committed and ai-rulez does not
rewrite the ignore file.

**Reason:** every one of the seven auto-included builtin domains either
restates a gate or contradicts it — complexity 20 versus ruff's 5, 120 columns
versus 88, 80% coverage versus 99%, "use conventional commits" versus the
blocking title check. A rule an agent obeys and a gate that fails it must never
be two separately maintained sentences, and per-domain exclusions would leave
the next release free to add a contradiction to a domain opted into. Off
entirely also keeps the generated file ~60 lines instead of ~270. ai-rulez's
default gitignore rewrite would break the cobo-sealed fence and hide the very
files GitHub must find in the repository.

**Rejected alternative:** per-domain `!` exclusions — the next-release risk.

agent-instructions.md#two-gates-plus-a-c.text:
prek runs the generator as a fixing hook; tox `style` runs `ai-rulez validate`;
and `ci.yml`'s hooks job additionally fails on any working-tree change
including untracked files. A template-ci scenario renders the toggle on with
*every* offered host, runs the generator, then the generated project's own
fixing hooks, and gates on `git diff`; it also runs the checking hooks and
gates on their exit codes. Checking hooks skip the paths a generator owns
(`.continue/prompts/` for trailing-whitespace, yamllint and the editorconfig
checker; `.mdc` for the editorconfig checker), rendered only under the toggle.

**Reason:** there is no check mode for preset output, and a fixing hook only
fails on a modified *tracked* file — a project that never committed its output
would have it regenerated untracked and stay green, shipping instructions that
exist on no branch. Two generators writing one tree that disagree on a byte
leave a repository that never converges. The defaults emit markdown alone and
converge; two hosts found only once the scenario covered every host do not —
continue-dev's YAML header carries trailing-space comment lines the whitespace
hook strips and the next generate restores, and cursor's `.mdc` rules fail the
editorconfig checker because the `\.md$` exclude does not reach the extra
character. A checking hook rejecting generated output cannot be satisfied at
all, so it gets the `.copier-answers.yml` answer: skip the generator-owned
path.

**Consequence:** the width of the gate is the width of the output it sees;
every offered host widens the scenario that must keep passing.

agent-instructions.md#no-claude-md-by-de.text:
The default shape uses `AGENTS.md` alone, including for Claude Code. The former
`@AGENTS.md` wrapper is neither rendered nor preserved on update any more, so
an update deletes leftover copies (customized ones too). `ai_rulez_presets`
defaults to `codex` and `copilot`; `claude` is still offered but not default;
`gemini` was removed from the choices.

**Reason:** Claude Code reads `AGENTS.md` natively, removing the only reason the
wrapper existed — and a leftover `CLAUDE.md` makes Claude Code's default mode
*skip* `AGENTS.md`, the opposite of what the default shape wants. The `codex`
host already writes `AGENTS.md`, so `claude` only added a duplicate wrapper and
a `.claude/` tree. The maintainers do not use Gemini and every offered host
widens the convergence scenario.

**Rejected alternative:** keep excluding `CLAUDE.md` from updates to protect
adopter guidance — kept a file that actively harmed the default; the README
tells adopters to move unique guidance first, and git history keeps the old
content.

**Consequence:** by default the per-host skills no longer reach Claude Code,
which looks under `.claude/skills/`; adopters who want them select `claude`.
Removing a choice has a sharp edge: a `--defaults` update (what Renovate runs)
silently replaces a recorded selection containing a removed choice with the new
defaults, so a project that selected `gemini` loses every other host too and
keeps a stale `GEMINI.md`; such a project cleans before updating and re-selects.

architecture-contracts.md#one-exhaustive.text:
import-linter is an always-on style tool. A single `layers` contract stacks
`cli` (present only with `include_cli`), the enabled non-CLI components as
pipe-separated independent siblings, then `core`, then `utils`. The contract
is `exhaustive`, so any subpackage not named in the layers breaks it;
non-layer foundations (`__main__`, `__metadata__`, `_version`, `_c_extension`)
are listed as exhaustive ignores.

**Reason:** components are gated on toggles and meant to be independent — a
`web -> gui` import is a latent bug against a sibling that may not be
installed — and none of the existing tools enforce which module may import
which. Sibling semantics give independence, layer order gives layering, and a
separate `cli` layer captures its legitimate lazy-import orchestration without
ignore rules. Exhaustiveness closes the gap that motivated the tool: coding
agents and hurried humans add a top-level package (`data/`, `marketplace/`)
that an unlisted-is-unconstrained contract ignored; prose in the agent
instructions does not hold, a failing style run does. `utils` below `core`
matches current reality and the conventional leaf-helpers model.

**Rejected alternative:** separate `independence` plus `layers` contracts —
redundant, and `independence` is degenerate with zero or one component, whereas
the single contract degrades to a valid `core > utils`.

**Consequence:** the contract is Jinja-conditional on enabled components, so a
component's coverage is exercised only when it is generated; the one boundary
it cannot forbid (`cli` importing MCP or worker) is harmless because `cli`
legitimately sits on top.

architecture-contracts.md#whole-program-.text:
import-linter and slotscheck (like basedpyright, mypy and sphinx-lint) run on
the prek gate as `local` `language = "system"` hooks that shell through
`uv run --locked --group style`, and in the tox `style` env from the same
group. Neither uses the upstream repo hook the tool ships.

**Reason:** both need the installed package and a whole-import-graph build
(grimp) or an import of every module (slotscheck). prek runs a repo hook in its
own isolated venv with only the hook's own deps, so the project is not
installed there and the graph cannot be built. A local system hook sees the
project's real environment, uses the single `style` pin (no second `rev` for
Renovate), and verified end-to-end that an injected upward import fails the
hook. slotscheck is worth the fast gate because it checks a property nothing
else covers; the redundant type checkers `ty`/`pyrefly`/`zuban` stay
style-env-only so five type checkers do not stack on every commit.

**Rejected alternative:** style-env-only for import-linter — an earlier revision
of the record, on the imprecise premise that prek cannot install the package;
true of the isolated repo-hook pattern, not of the local system hook.

ci-topology.md#network-dependent-checks-.text:
Checks whose outcome depends on the network or on an upstream that can change
without a commit here — docs link checking, the cobo gitignore drift check, the
template's generated-artifact drift check — run on a weekly `schedule` plus
`workflow_dispatch`, never on `pull_request`, and never join the `check`
aggregation. They surface rot as a visible, non-blocking workflow result; a tox
env or mise task lets a maintainer run each on demand.

**Reason:** a transient 5xx, a rate limit, a site blocking CI, or an upstream
boilerplate update must never block an unrelated merge. A weekly signal is the
right cadence for drift that accumulates slowly, and a PR-time check cannot see
drift caused by something that changed underneath the repository.

**Rejected alternative:** run them on pull requests — flaky red checks on
unrelated changes.

ci-topology.md#a-single-union-coverage-g.text:
Each matrix cell combined its per-interpreter data, kept a non-gating report,
and uploaded a per-OS artifact; one `coverage-combine` job merged every cell
and was the only place `fail_under = 99` was enforced, measuring the union of
all OS and interpreter cells. `relative_files = true` made data from different
runners mergeable, complementing the `src`/`site-packages` path remap. The
combined XML became the one Codecov upload.

**Reason:** per-cell gating measured each OS alone, so a line covered on Linux
but gated off on Windows was reported inconsistently, and there was no
authoritative cross-fan-out number. The union is the correct scope. This held
while the matrix was symmetric — every cell measured the same code.

**Consequence:** once the CI job split into path-filtered per-component jobs, a
skipped component dropped its subtree from the union and the single gate failed
on every partial PR; the principle survives per component in the successor.

ci-topology.md#a-tokenless-public-html-c.text:
`include_smokeshow` (default off, `full` preset) adds a step that uploads the
HTML report to an ephemeral public URL with no secret. It runs only on public
repositories, last in the coverage job, and is best-effort
(`continue-on-error`).

**Reason:** Codecov is opt-in and non-blocking, so a self-contained project had
no hosted, browsable coverage report; smokeshow gives a public project one
without an account. Its tokenless endpoint has low rate limits, so a transient
failure must neither fail the job that feeds the required `check` gate nor
abort the authoritative Codecov upload; a private report must never be
published.

ci-topology.md#per-component-markers-pat.text:
One pytest marker per enabled component plus `core`, applied automatically by a
root `conftest.py` hook from each test's top-level `tests/<dir>/`. A
`changes` path-filter job emits one boolean per component plus `core`; the
monolithic CI job splits into `test-core` (always) and `test-<component>` jobs
gated on their own filter or `core`. Each `coverage-<component>` job merges
that component's OS cells and enforces `fail_under = 99` scoped to its subtree
via `--include`; `coverage-core` uses `--omit` of every component and re-adds
`*/_version.py` because a CLI `--omit` overrides the pyproject one. A
non-gating `coverage-report` job merges what ran, omitting skipped components so
their unexecuted files are not reported at zero, and publishes to Codecov,
smokeshow and SonarCloud. The `check` gate lists every path-gated job as an
allowed skip. The default `tox run` is unchanged.

**Reason:** every component's suite ran on every OS for a one-line change in
another component, and a contributor had no knob to run only one component.
`core` is the escape hatch — it watches dependencies, the shared `core/` tree,
root modules and root tests, so a change underpinning every component forces
the full fan-out, mirroring the import layering. Per-component skipping is
incompatible with a single union gate, so the gate is decomposed; skipping is
sound because an unchanged subtree has nothing to regress. The cross-OS union
is kept *within* a component, where a per-cell gate would wrongly fail on a
platform-gated branch. The aggregation action counts a skipped job as a
failure unless named, hence the allowed-skips list rendered from the same
component list as `needs`.

**Consequence:** a full run fans out to more jobs than before; the win is on
component-scoped PRs. `--include`/`--omit` patterns must match both the
editable and installed layouts (`*/`-anchored) and are verifiable only through a
real `tox run`. Adding a component touches the marker list, the conftest
directory set, the filters, two jobs and the omit list in lockstep.

ci-topology.md#asymmetric-matrix-every-i.text:
Each `test-*` job runs Python 3.10 through 3.14 on Ubuntu and the invoking
interpreter on macOS and Windows; with `include_c_extensions` every OS runs all
five. `style` runs once on Ubuntu, with mypy additionally run for the win32
and darwin platforms. With `include_cli`, a `cli-installed` job runs the
installed console-script check on all three OSes. Explicit tox env lists keep
style and CLI execution out of the component jobs.

**Reason:** cross-platform behaviour needs every OS at one interpreter and
interpreter compatibility needs every interpreter on one OS; the full
cross-product repeats two mostly independent dimensions. Type checkers prune
`sys.platform` branches against their host, so the platform flags keep static
coverage of platform-gated code. Marker arguments forwarded to pytest must not
reach the `cli` tox env, which would call the installed command with pytest's
`-m` option instead of its default argument.

**Consequence:** a defect needing one particular non-Linux OS and a
non-representative interpreter may pass CI — the accepted cost.

ci-topology.md#every-generated-ci-job-sk.text:
Every job in `ci.yml` carries the falsy-safe condition that the pull request is
not a draft, composed with existing conditions rather than replacing them
(`check` keeps `always()`, SonarCloud its fork guard, component jobs their
change filters). The `pull_request` trigger explicitly includes
`ready_for_review`. Security and docs-preview workflows still run on drafts.

**Reason:** drafts paid for the whole fan-out before review. `!= true` keeps
running on push and manual events where the pull-request object is absent,
unlike `== false`. Without `ready_for_review`, a PR opened as a draft could
stay permanently skipped after becoming reviewable. Draft PRs skip `check`
itself, so they need no allowed-skip entry.

components.md#secondary-components-are-s.text:
The highest-precedence enabled component (CLI > GUI > TUI > web > MCP > worker,
spelled once as `primary_component` in `copier.yml`) owns the bare `<pkg>`
command. Every other enabled component is a lazily imported subcommand
(`interactive`, `gui`, `web`, `mcp`, `worker`); no `<pkg>-<name>` console
script is emitted. A root exists only where it buys something, captured by the
hidden `include_console_root`: with `include_cli`, with web, or with two or more
components. With no root, bare `<pkg>` dispatches to the sole component from
`__main__`. GUI uses `[project.gui-scripts]` only as the sole runnable
component; a GUI primary sharing a root gets a normal console script.

**Reason:** a multi-component project installed four or five sibling
executables, a separate script is invisible until you know its name, and the
CLI already exposed `interactive`/`gui`/`web` subcommands beside their suffixed
scripts while MCP and worker had none. A windowless launcher as the shared root
would swallow console I/O and `--help` of the subcommands on Windows. One
computed variable is the single source for the `cli/` package, the `typer`
dependency, the import-linter orchestrator layer and the `__main__` branch, so
`typer` stays off a single-component non-CLI app.

**Rejected alternative:** a universal root for every app — forces `typer` onto
single-component non-CLI apps and dilutes what `include_cli` means.

**Rejected alternative:** keep suffixed scripts when no CLI is present — leaves
the PATH and discoverability problem for non-CLI multi-component apps.

**Consequence:** the package directory is named `cli/` even in a launcher-only
project; adopters updating lose the suffixed scripts and switch wrappers to the
subcommand form.

components.md#cli-framework-offers-argpa.text:
A `cli_framework` sub-question (`typer` default, `argparse`), asked only with
`include_cli`, mirrors `web_framework`. The argparse root is standard-library
only and contract-equivalent: same `version`/`info` commands, same lazily
imported component subcommands, help on no arguments, non-zero exit on missing
metadata. A no-CLI launcher keeps the Typer root. The `typer` entry in

components.md#launcher-imports-are-guard.text:
Each launcher's lazy import is wrapped in a context manager that turns a
`ModuleNotFoundError` whose name is *exactly* one of the component's declared
dependency modules into an exit-1 message naming the component, the module and
the fix (`uv sync`). Dependencies that import late (uvicorn, Tkinter, textual)
or re-export behind their own guard with no module name (faststream brokers,
mcp's transitive imports) are imported eagerly inside the block by a preflight
that re-raises with the caller-supplied name. Tkinter gets a system-package
hint (including a version-qualified Homebrew formula) because it is not a
distribution. The root's own module-scope imports (`typer`, pydantic via the
settings stack) and the sole-component entrypoint in `__main__.py` get the same
treatment; all derived facts are `when: false` computed variables in
`copier.yml`.

**Reason:** there are no extras to name — component deps are core dependencies —
so a missing module means the environment is out of sync with the metadata and
`uv sync` is the honest remedy. The first-party import always succeeds after a
`copier update`; the third-party failure happens one frame deeper, so the guard
must classify what comes out of the import rather than replace it. Exact
matching protects application defects (a typo'd import below an installed
dependency) from being mislabelled as a stale environment. The sole-component
entrypoint is what frozen binaries target, whose user has no CLI to fall back
on. Shared computed variables matter most for the two guards rendered into
different files, only one of which exists in any project.

the issue proposed — no extra exists, and replacing the first-party import would
not catch the deeper failure.

**Rejected alternative:** guard every component's module scope so direct library
imports also get the message — the reader is already in a traceback in their
own code, the guard would run on every successful import forever, and component
modules are what adopters edit most.

**Rejected alternative:** let faststream's own `ImportError` through — its advice
(`pip install "faststream[<broker>]"`) bypasses the lockfile.

`<pkg> run [module:attribute]` starts the web app on the configured bind;
`<pkg> dev` adds autoreload and forces a loopback bind. Both share one private
runner and the dependency guard; `<pkg> web` stays as an alias where web is not
primary. The target is passed to uvicorn as an import string, validated for
shape only — no module search, no framework sniffing. `include_console_root`
now includes `include_web`, so a web-only project reaches its component through
the minimal launcher.

framework CLI per framework that the project's own help never mentioned.
uvicorn is already a web runtime dependency and takes an import string with
reload natively; the string form is the only one that can reload in a child
process, so one code path serves both modes. A reloading server executes
unreviewed code on every save and belongs on loopback. A web-only project had
no root to hang a verb on, and standalone `<pkg>-run`/`<pkg>-dev` scripts are
the second entry scheme the subcommand decision exists to prevent.

`faststream[cli]` at runtime, which the template deliberately keeps out of
`dependencies`, and type-sniffing the target is the framework detection avoided
here.

**Rejected alternative:** replace `<pkg> web` with `<pkg> run` — breaks the one
naming rule the subcommand decision makes.

**Rejected alternative:** let uvicorn parse the target — its error names no
project command and is not testable the way a cheap shape check is.

entrypoint is the console root.

`core/app.py` exposes three functions — `version()` and `info()`, which raise

never raises — plus the error type and an unknown-version constant. Each
component imports the module as `service` and adapts: the CLI exits 1, the web
app answers 503, the MCP tool returns error text, GUI and TUI show "unknown",

component is enabled. One `missing_metadata` fixture patching

is already that layer. Functions rather than a class because it would hold no
state and ruff's no-self-use rule flags exactly that shape; no Protocol because

because there are three real behaviours, each with more than one caller.

model keeps its own platform fields because routing them through a dict adds
indirection for no sharing.

a `VersionProvider` protocol, as proposed — each adds a name without adding a
constraint.

files than the three f-strings they would hold.

docs-stack.md#sphinx-warnings-use-an-exa.text:
The docs-build gate captures Sphinx warnings and compares them with a committed
allowlist. It rejects both new unexpected warnings and expected warnings that
are no longer emitted. The default allowlist is empty. Normalization removes
machine-specific path prefixes and folds Windows separators, while preserving
line numbers. Sphinx's `nitpicky` mode remains off.

**Reason:** an individually justified upstream warning should not force a choice
between permanently red documentation builds and broad warning suppression.
Exact entries make exceptions reviewable; the reverse comparison prevents
obsolete exceptions from accumulating silently.

**Rejected alternative:** make every warning fatal directly through Sphinx's
warning-as-error mode. It was superseded by the allowlist so unavoidable
exceptions can coexist with a regression gate.

**Alternative deferred:** enable `nitpicky` immediately. The issue anticipated
a noisy initial cross-reference cleanup and left this for a separate pass.
Removing line numbers was also considered but not selected; no further reason
for that choice was established in the reviewed sources.

with `literalinclude` and imported or called by the regular pytest suite. The
directory is in scope for ruff, every type checker and pylint, but outside the

code, hence outside coverage.

let a broken README doctest pass locally and surface only in CI.

curated Markdown surface; neither collector overlaps the other.

docs-versioning.md#docs-publish-only-the.text:
A generated `tools/build_docs.py` computes the version slug, enumerates the
version directories already on `gh-pages`, writes a generated (gitignored)
`versions.json` for Shibuya's native switcher, builds only the current ref,
copies every other version directory across from `gh-pages`, writes a root
redirect to `latest` (the highest non-prerelease by PEP 440 ordering), and
deploys with previews excluded from cleaning. Versioned publishing is how a
docs-enabled project always publishes; it is not a toggle. The version list is
stateless: `gh-pages` is the source of truth, and local builds hide the
switcher because no `versions.json` exists.

**Reason:** `sphinx-multiversion` (effectively unmaintained) and
`sphinx-polyversion` both rebuild every selected tag on every deploy. This
template's `conf.py` runs subprocess generators against the live app, so
rebuilding a historical tag re-runs that tag's generators against whatever the
build resolves — fragile, slow, and it forces every past `conf.py` to keep
building forever. Litestar's build-current-preserve-rest model avoids that.
Litestar commits and hand-edits its version list, which is untenable with
per-minor granularity and automated releases, and having CI commit back to a
protected `main` adds real machinery.

**Rejected alternative:** `sphinx-multiversion` or `sphinx-polyversion` — the
rebuild model above.

**Rejected alternative:** a committed `versions.json` — the hand-edit or
CI-commit cost above.

**Consequence:** `gh-pages` becomes load-bearing state; both deploy paths must
preserve the numeric version-slug directories. An older version's switcher is
frozen at its build time, so the switcher appears only from the first versioned
release onward.

gitignore-generation.md#the-fence-is-lf-.text:
The fence is sealed with cobo's `--eol lf` policy, persisted as `eol = "lf"` on
the lock fragment. The macOS boilerplate encodes two filenames that end in a
carriage return (`Icon␍`, `.HFS+ Private Directory Data␍`) as single-line
character classes; LF normalization splits each into an unterminated `Icon[`
(matches nothing, inert) and an orphan `]` (ignores a file literally named
`]`). Those two patterns are knowingly broken in every generated project.

**Reason:** the template enforces LF everywhere (`.gitattributes`,
EditorConfig, ruff), `editorconfig-checker` fails on an embedded CR, and —
decisively — Copier renders `.gitignore.jinja` through Jinja, whose lexer
normalizes a lone `\r` to `\n` at scaffold time. A byte-exact (`preserve`) seal
would therefore report `locally modified` forever in every generated project.
There is no LF-only pattern that matches `Icon␍` precisely (`Icon?` over-matches),
so fidelity genuinely requires the CR, and the CR cannot survive the render.
These are legacy HFS resource-fork artifacts modern macOS rarely creates and
almost never commits — an accepted tradeoff, not "harmless".

**Rejected alternative:** seal byte-exact and keep the CR — fights the LF
invariant and is re-corrupted by the render anyway.

**Consequence:** the cobo-level fix is necessary but not sufficient; restoring
the patterns additionally needs a render that preserves the CR (a raw wrap or a
Copier newline carve-out scoped to this file).

`include_homebrew` and `include_scoop` are independent toggles, off by default
and asked only when the project can distribute natively. When enabled,
`release.yml` gains `bump-homebrew`/`bump-scoop` jobs that fire a

or bucket does the manifest work with each ecosystem's own tooling; the
generated project ships a reference listener and setup guide under

workflow. The listener opens its own PR with its own token, so the PAT needs no
pull-request scope.

generated project — the original design of this record, replaced for the
duplication above.

one ecosystem only.

fallback is best-effort because Scoop's tooling assumes binary downloads; the

listener's job.

release-automation.md#release-please-is-.text:
Every generated project ships an unconditional release-please pipeline in one
unified `release.yml`: Conventional Commits on `main` open a release PR, its
merge cuts the tag and release, and every downstream job (build, PyPI,
executables, Docker, docs, SBOM, notifications) gates on its outputs. The
former `release_automation` choice (`none`, release-please, release-it,
release-drafter) and the separate `cd.yml` are gone. Versioning is sourced from
git tags through hatch-vcs, so release-please never edits a version literal and
`uv.lock` cannot desync; `bump-minor-pre-major` keeps pre-1.0 projects pre-1.0.

**Reason:** offering three tools multiplied the integration surface for a
feature each project configures once. release-please is Python-native, derives
the version from commits the template already enforces, and produces a
reviewable release PR before any tag exists. Two of the three hard-won keycast
fixes were already in the template, so it was the option with the most
evidence.

**Rejected alternative:** release-it — JS-oriented, needs a Node runtime, and a
human picks the bump every time.

**Rejected alternative:** release-drafter — label-driven, writes release notes
but no `CHANGELOG.md`.

**Rejected alternative:** keeping a `none` escape hatch — projects that want no
automation delete the files after generation; accepted for a template whose
audience publishes releases.

**Consequence:** the PyPI trusted publisher must register `release.yml` as the
workflow. Rendering plus actionlint validate the workflow across option
combinations, but draft-tag timing, OIDC publishing and reconciliation can only
be exercised by a live release. The template has no `CHANGELOG.md` seed file:
release-please owns the changelog, and a scaffold-time seed would wipe an
adopting project's release history on update.

release-automation.md#the-release-is-cre.text:
release-please creates the GitHub release with `draft: true` and
`force-tag-creation: true`. Build jobs attach wheels, executables and the SBOM
to the draft; `finalize-release` un-drafts it and then closes the phantom
next-release PR and re-dispatches the workflow, bounded.

**Reason:** a public release must never exist without its artifacts, so the
release stays a draft until they are attached. GitHub withholds a draft's git
tag until publication, so without forced tag creation the build job would run
before the tag exists and hatch-vcs would stamp the previous version. The
phantom PR exists because release-please computes its commit range from the
latest *published* release and ignores drafts.

**Rejected alternative:** `draft: false` — a window with a public release and no
artifacts.

**Consequence:** docs deployment lives in the same workflow (`deploy-docs`,
after finalization) because an event fired by `finalize-release`'s token cannot
trigger a separate workflow.

release-automation.md#the-workflow-dispa.text:
`release.yml` keeps `workflow_dispatch`. The publish jobs run in a `publish`
environment whose deployment-branch policy is limited to `main`; the generated
setup guide ships that policy as a scriptable step with a check, because GitHub
auto-creates the environment unprotected on first use.

**Reason:** the trigger looks like a publish-escalation surface — a manual run
executes the workflow file from the selected branch, so the `release_created`
guard cannot stop someone with write access from dispatching a guard-free copy
and minting a trusted-publishing token. But `finalize-release`'s reconciliation
re-dispatches the workflow through the API, which requires the trigger.
GitHub evaluates an environment's branch policy outside the workflow file, so
the environment contains what the trigger exposes.

**Rejected alternative:** remove the trigger — breaks release-PR reconciliation.

release-automation.md#release-workflows-.text:
Release-please runs with the implicit `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Two consequences are
handled procedurally in the generated setup guide rather than with a stronger
credential: the release PR reports no required status contexts until a human
closes and reopens it, and a merge that changes workflow files between the
release PR merging and the release run finishing must wait, because the
release API then refuses tag creation with a 403.

**Reason:** events created with the workflow token do not start workflow runs,
and the token cannot be granted workflow write access. A PAT or App token would
fix both but is a standing credential with write access to `main`; closing and
reopening the PR (every required context listens for `reopened`) and pausing
workflow merges are the cheaper side of that trade. Editing the PR body is not
equivalent — two of the checks do not listen for `edited`.

**Rejected alternative:** a PAT or GitHub App token for release-please.

release-automation.md#the-release-automa.text:
Two friction points reopened the tool choice: a stable release cut after
release candidates lists only changes since the last RC (release-please has no
prerelease/stable distinction and no config remedy; the npm CLI team works
around the same behaviour by hand), and the draft-then-finalize dance plus
phantom-PR reconciliation are workarounds layered on release-please's model.
The research frames tools as commit helpers, changelog engines and release
orchestrators, and compares Commitizen (`cz bump`, fixes the RC range with one
setting, medium effort, reverses the commit-helper decision, loses the
reviewable release PR) against git-cliff (a changelog engine only; high effort,
RC math stays hand-written). Four options stand: stay and document, migrate to
Commitizen, git-cliff inside a bespoke orchestrator, or defer. Until decided,
nothing changes.

**Why this needs an answer:** both replacements need a standing privileged
credential or a maintainer-local bump under the `full` preset's ruleset, and
`release.yml` fans out to every generated project while being validated only
by rendering until a live release runs. Whether the RC gap bites often enough
to justify that blast radius is a maintainer judgement, not a research result.

Docker Hub publication is optional and its credential pair is all-or-nothing:
neither credential means GHCR-only publication, both enable Docker Hub, and a
partial pair fails a shared preflight before either PyPI or Docker publication.

**Reason:** PyPI uploads are irreversible. A credential check inside only the
Docker job would allow PyPI publication to finish concurrently before Docker
failed, stranding a partially published release. The shared prerequisite rejects
that known configuration error before the publish jobs fan out; it does not make
all later external uploads transactional.

**Rejected alternative:** validate the credentials only inside Docker
publication. Review moved the check into a shared prerequisite specifically to
prevent the PyPI race. Requiring Docker Hub for every web release is not the
selected contract; GHCR-only publication remains supported.

The narrowly scoped ghalint exceptions exist because conditional steps need
job-scoped credential-presence information and GitHub does not expose the
secrets context directly in conditions. The token itself is reduced to a
presence flag, not exposed job-wide. The exceptions are recorded in the
generated `.github/ghalint.yaml` rather than disabling that policy globally.

declarative, export-friendly file, which weakens the earlier duplication
concern.

repo-setup.md#a-resume-driven-repo-setup.text:
Every actionable step in the setup doc carries a `[CHECK]` block: a command
where exit 0 means the step is done. End-state checks assert the state a step
establishes (not a weaker proxy); secret-presence checks assert the stored
artifact by name, with conditional variants gated on repository attributes;
steps with no API-visible artifact carry an explicit no-scriptable-check
marker; steps covered by another step point at it. A skill shipped verbatim
into every generated project walks the doc top to bottom without aborting,
classifies steps as required, deferred (GitHub Pages and previews, expected red
until the first release) or optional (asks configure-or-skip), and reports
everything together. A symmetric repo-local skill drives this repository's own
two-step setup inline, flagging its deliberate `write`-not-`read` workflow
permission.

**Reason:** the prose was executed two lossy ways — a human hand-running
commands, or an external plugin skill with its own hand-maintained verify list
duplicating the doc. Neither knew per step whether it was already done, and
setup is invisible to CI. A standalone `steps.yaml` manifest would re-encode the
commands, actor tags and Jinja gating the doc already carries and drift against
it — exactly what the single-home decision collapsed. The consumer is an LLM
reader, not a parser, so RST readability suffices. Deferred classification is
the fix for a naive walk deadlocking at Pages before reaching the rest. The
skill is a rendered file, so it never needs a post-copy task.

**Rejected alternative:** a `steps.yaml` manifest — the drift above.

**Consequence:** every future setup step must carry a `[CHECK]` block to stay
machine-drivable, as every step already had to carry an actor tag.

runtime-logging.md#an-unavailable-home-d.text:
Logging attaches the console handler before attempting file logging. Failure to
resolve the home directory disables file logging entirely; file-system errors
with a resolved home also degrade to console-only logging. Directory values may
still use a temporary-directory-derived `Path` as a placeholder, but the template
does not automatically write logs there.

**Reason:** logger initialization can happen at module import, so unavailable or
unwritable home storage must not crash read-only commands. A predictable shared
temporary log path can be pre-created or symlinked by another local user; its
existence as a valid `Path` does not establish safe ownership for writes.

**Rejected alternative:** automatically log under a shared temporary project
directory when home resolution fails. The initial fallback was explicitly
rejected because it creates a local log-hijacking opportunity.

Lazy file-handler initialization was suggested, but the reviewed evidence does
not establish why it was not selected. The current cached logger accessor also
does not make module-level calls lazy: caching prevents repeated setup, not the
first import-time initialization.

`include_launcher` (PyCrucible, uv-bootstrap launcher), `include_compiler`
(Nuitka, source-to-machine-code) and `include_freezer` (PyInstaller,

one of three architectures that make materially different promises — a tiny

the tool means swapping PyCrucible for PyApp later needs no variable rename.

executable. PyOxidizer — archived.

migration (Copier does not rename variables). Build dependencies live in the uv
`tool` group and are Renovate-tracked like every other pin. Each toggle must be
exercised independently and in combination.

standalone-executables.md#executables-ar.text:
Each build names its binary `<pkg>-<tool>-<os-label>` rather than a bare
`<pkg>`. All three builds target the package's `__main__.py`, which was
generalized from a CLI-only form into the single entry that selects and
launches whichever component is enabled; with an executable toggle on but no
runnable component selected, `main()` raises a `SystemExit` with an
explanatory message.

**Reason:** the release job collects every executable artifact with
`merge-multiple`, which flattens by filename — bare names made per-OS (and,
with more than one toggle, per-tool) binaries silently overwrite each other and
drop platforms from the release. One entrypoint keeps the PyInstaller spec, the
Nuitka command and the PyCrucible config free of duplicated component
conditionals and guarantees the binary *runs* the app rather than importing a
module that never invokes it. A binary that builds and exits non-zero with a
reason beats one that silently does nothing and looks broken.

**Consequence:** PyCrucible takes the name via its output option, Nuitka via
`--output-filename` (otherwise a generic `__main__.bin`), PyInstaller is renamed
after the build because its spec cannot see the CI matrix. The PyInstaller spec
is rendered for reproducible builds and un-ignored in the generated
`.gitignore` (the default `*.spec` ignore would keep it uncommitted and break
the fresh-checkout release build); Nuitka's flags live in the mise task and CI
step since it has no spec equivalent. The mise `package` task was split per
architecture, which also fixed a latent bug where the whole `mise.toml` body
sat in one raw block and rendered the PyCrucible task regardless of the toggle.

supply-chain-security.md#provenance-mint.text:
The release build attests the distributions it produces and retains the
provenance bundles alongside the release artifacts. Matrix builds attest their
own outputs. Attestation minting runs behind the same externally protected
`publish` environment as package publication, with a main-only deployment policy
configured during repository setup. Referencing the environment in workflow
source alone does not prove that an adopter configured its live policy.
Consumer verification identifies
the release workflow and the `main` ref, not only the repository. The workflow
enables attestation for public repositories and requires explicit opt-in for
private ones.

**Reason:** repository identity alone does not prove that the intended protected
release workflow built an artifact. A branch-dispatched workflow could otherwise
mint repository-backed attestations for arbitrary outputs. GitHub evaluates the
environment's deployment policy outside the dispatched workflow file, so that
boundary also protects provenance minting. The private opt-in avoids breaking
releases on plans without the necessary attestation support.

**Rejected alternative:** leave minting in an unprotected build job and verify
only repository identity. Review rejected this weaker trust boundary.

**Rejected alternative:** attempt attestations unconditionally on private
repositories. Review required explicit opt-in to preserve unsupported private
release paths.

records why its signer constraints and the minting boundary exist.

supply-chain-security.md#relationship-be.text:
The proposal asked whether the trusted-publishing action's PEP 740 attestations
make the explicit GitHub provenance step partly redundant, or whether both paths
serve a deliberate belt-and-suspenders purpose. The implementation retains the
GitHub path, but the rationale for its relationship to PyPI-side attestations
could not be recovered. No historical reason for keeping both was established;
this was not a finding that either mechanism was defective or safe to remove.

The current decision below resolves the configuration choice from verified
technical differences. It does not turn that new justification into a claim
about the original implementation's intent.

supply-chain-security.md#retain-build-pr.text:
The current configuration retains both mechanisms. GitHub's build step produces
SLSA provenance at build time, with workflow/source/run information and artifact
digests. The pinned PyPI action defaults to a PyPI Publish attestation during
Trusted Publishing to PyPI or TestPyPI: its predicate body is empty, and its
certificate identity identifies the publisher. It is not a second structured
SLSA build statement. PEP 740 defines index-hosted attestation handling rather
than requiring that all attestations make the same claim.

**Reason:** the claims and consumer channels complement one another. GitHub
stores build attestations and the template attaches their bundles to releases;
PyPI exposes publication attestations through its per-file provenance APIs and
UI. The publishing and release-attachment jobs download the built distributions
without rebuilding them, preserving the artifact hashes. PyPI's default signing
does not export the separately created GitHub build-provenance bundle to PyPI.

**Rejected alternative:** remove the explicit GitHub step because PyPI already
signs attestations. The default publication claim does not replace the structured
build claim or the build bundle distributed with GitHub Releases.

**Rejected alternative:** disable PyPI's default attestations as duplicate work.
That would remove the index-hosted publication claim and its discovery channel.
There is overlapping identity/integrity coverage, but neither path currently
replaces all of the other's claims and availability.

directories and asserts on the output tree: every preset renders, plus one

far cheaper property, so the two layers stay separate.

template-testing.md#generated-files-must.text:
A generated file must already be in the exact byte form the generated project's
own formatters produce — yamlfmt, ruff-format, the prek builtins and taplo.
Three things follow: formatter config is chosen so the hand-written layout is
canonical (`retain_line_breaks_single` for yamlfmt; no array auto-expand,
auto-collapse or comment alignment for taplo; no yamlfmt `max_line_length`);
template sources are written in that form (one-line folded scalars, no comment
trailing a sequence, TOML arrays one-per-line with trailing comma, Jinja
whitespace control so no conditional leaves more than two blank lines or one at
EOF, literal UTF-8 author tokens instead of `tojson`); and taplo runs in strict
check mode. `template-ci.yml`'s render job runs the rendered project's own
fixing hooks per scenario and gates on `git diff`, with an `integrations`
scenario and a non-ASCII author name covering toggles nothing else rendered.

**Reason:** on a pristine scaffold the first hook run rewrote two workflow files
and taplo rewrote two TOML files while exiting 0, so the adopter's `hooks` CI
failed and every later `copier update` showed drift they never caused. Nothing
caught it because this repo ran only checking tools over a render and the
harness asserts YAML parses, not that it is canonical; taplo's fix mode made the
defect invisible. Width-driven reflow would make a file's canonical form depend
on which components are enabled, and comment alignment would let a Renovate
bump break a line nothing touched. The diff, not hook exit codes, is the gate
because a fixing hook that rewrites and exits 0 sails through an exit-code
check.

**Rejected alternative:** chase the formatters' output in the templates — the
config is pinned to make the written layout canonical instead.

**Consequence:** hand-aligned trailing comments and hand-wrapped folded scalars
are unavailable; a conditional block in rendered YAML/TOML requires thinking
about whitespace control; the pinned knobs fail loudly if a release changes
them.

`copier` manager, which watches the template's git tags, runs the real
`copier update` and opens a PR. No bespoke workflow ships. This repository's
own release-please therefore must keep cutting tags — they are the datasource.
Scaffolding uses the `.git` HTTPS URL because the `gh:` shorthand is not a git
URL and the `git-tags` datasource rejects it silently.

**Reason:** nothing in a generated project watched for template changes and the
template published no tags, so a default `copier update` found nothing. The
template already ships Renovate as the canonical updater; its App token can
push workflow files (the repo `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot), and its PRs flow through
the existing dashboard and review. Tags are cheap since release-please already
runs and give adopters a changelog besides.

**Rejected alternative:** a bespoke `copier-update.yml` workflow — ~50 lines of
security-sensitive YAML per project, and its default token cannot push
`.github/workflows/*`, forcing every consumer to provision a PAT.

**Rejected alternative:** `fohte/copier-update-action` — the bespoke workflow as
a third-party action, same token and conflict characteristics, plus an external
action to trust with `--trust`.

**Rejected alternative:** drop the template's own versioning and track HEAD —
the copier manager is tag-based, so release-please is the price of Renovate.

**Consequence:** a copier-update PR can look mergeable while carrying conflict

template-updates.md#shipped-template-pin.text:
A `packageRules` entry in `.github/renovate.json` matches `template/**` and
disables updates there. Shipped version literals (action SHAs, prek `rev` pins,
mise tool versions, dependency pins) are seed values only; each generated
project's own Renovate owns them afterwards. This repository's root workflows,
`prek.toml` and `mise.toml` stay Renovate-managed.

**Reason:** `copier update` is a 3-way merge per file, and a pinned line
conflicts when both sides moved it to different values. Both repositories'
bots advanced the same literals on independent schedules, so copier-update PRs
conflicted on nearly every release — and Renovate does not fail on those
conflicts, so a PR looked mergeable with markers inside. With the template
frozen, "theirs" equals "base" on every pin line and the downstream's value
wins cleanly: the conflict class is eliminated structurally. `matchFileNames`
plus `enabled: false` rather than `ignorePaths` preserves the shared preset's
own ignore list and composes with its digest-pinning policy.

**Rejected alternative:** auto-resolve in the downstream's favour via a
`merge=ours` driver or copier `_exclude` — `_exclude` is whole-file and would
block genuine template changes; a per-downstream merge driver is fragile.

**Rejected alternative:** converge by cadence (group bumps, release
immediately) — only shrinks the race window.

**Consequence:** new projects start with slightly stale but valid seeds and
their own Renovate opens catch-up PRs; refreshing seeds before a release is a
deliberate act that reintroduces conflicts for projects not yet caught up.
Re-enabling Renovate for `template/**` reads as fixing staleness but rebuilds
the conflict engine.

template-updates.md#adoption-audits-pres.text:
The shipped adoption skill treats template defaults as evidence to compare with
existing project behavior, rather than automatic authority to replace it.
It handles initial adoption, updates, and audits of already-committed updates;
repository-settings changes remain the responsibility of `repo-setup`.

**Reason:** two workflows that both run prek can differ in event coverage and
required-check identity. Consolidating them can discard manual dispatch or leave
live branch protection waiting for a check that no longer exists. A local
ruleset file alone cannot establish the live requirements. A post-update audit
can compare the actual committed baseline and diff without rerunning Copier and
disturbing the state being inspected.

**Alternatives considered:** retain both workflows, accepting duplicate PR
execution, or consolidate after preserving event coverage and transitioning the
required check. The documented walkthrough deliberately makes that choice
conditional on the adopter's decision and evidence; neither option is rejected
universally. Deletion without establishing equivalence is excluded because it
can silently remove functionality or block merges.

The execution procedure is in `docs/template-adoption.md`.

Copier renders this template. Generated projects carry a `.copier-answers.yml`
and pull later template changes with `copier update`.

**Reason:** native update support matters most for a template that keeps
evolving — adopters pull new features, CI improvements and dependency updates
instead of re-applying them by hand. Conditional file inclusion via filename
patterns is cleaner than hook-based approaches, the answers file makes updates
reproducible, and full Jinja2 (whitespace control, raw blocks for GitHub Actions
syntax) is required by the workflow templates. Copier is actively maintained and
aligned with the uv/hatchling ecosystem the generated projects use.

**Rejected alternative:** Cookiecutter — the largest ecosystem, but no native
update/sync; pulling upstream changes is manual work.

**Rejected alternative:** Cruft — adds `cruft update`/`cruft check` on top of
Cookiecutter, but as a wrapper it is limited by Cookiecutter's internals.

**Rejected alternative:** Yeoman — JavaScript-based, not Python-native, heavier
runtime dependency.

**Rejected alternative:** GitHub template repositories — no variable
substitution and no conditional logic.

**Consequence:** adopters need `copier` installed; the template ecosystem is
smaller than Cookiecutter's; syntax differs slightly (`copier.yml`).

testing-strategy.md#the-worker-exposes-a.text:
`worker/app.py` provides `build_broker(url=None)`, which resolves the
connection at call time (argument, broker-specific env var, local default) and
registers the subscriber and publisher on the broker it returns; a module-level

publisher are factory-local closures, so the unit test asserts on a response
delivered to a collector subscriber rather than importing internals.

so the driver loads at import regardless of where the statement sits. The real
blocker to integration testing was *construction at import time* — a
localhost-bound singleton tests cannot retarget. The factory is the seam a real
round-trip test needs: a fresh broker pointed at a throwaway instance, no
import-order games.

one clean return type, and tests should observe behaviour, not wiring.

testing-strategy.md#real-broker-integrat.text:
An `integration`-marked test round-trips a message through the real driver. It
is deselected from the default suite and run by an on-demand tox env and a
conditional, Ubuntu-only `worker-integration` CI job keyed to the one chosen
broker. Container startup lives in a plain context manager: when the broker's
URL env var is already set it connects directly; otherwise it starts a
testcontainer. In CI, redis and nats use runner-provided `services:`
containers (the split lives once, as the `ci_service` field on
`worker_broker_spec` in `copier.yml`, with `health_cmd: null` marking "no
usable in-container probe"); kafka and rabbitmq keep testcontainers. The env
runs with a broad deprecation-warning demotion and a pytest timeout.

**Reason:** the in-memory test broker stubs out exactly the things that regress
— serialization, connection handling, driver compatibility — and CI never
started a broker. Docker is reliably available only on Ubuntu runners, so the
cross-OS matrix must stay Docker-free. testcontainers owns the lifecycle from
the test, so a laptop run matches CI. The original reasoning over-generalized
against `services:`: for fast-starting brokers the runner starts, health-gates
and injects the connection before the job, which is lighter than in-test
orchestration; Kafka's advertised listeners and RabbitMQ's readiness are not
worth that path. NATS runs without a health check because its monitoring
endpoint needs a container command that service containers cannot set, and
the test's own connect-retry covers readiness. A context manager rather than a
fixture because a fixture consumed only by a deselected test reads as unused to
the dead-fixtures check in `style`. Module-scoping the warning demotion was
tried and rejected: CLI `-W` module matching is exact, and drivers attribute
warnings via `stacklevel` to arbitrary caller frames.

**Rejected alternative:** `services:` for every broker — static YAML without
per-test lifecycle, and Kafka/RabbitMQ readiness is not worth it.

**Rejected alternative:** a fan-out over all four brokers — a generated project
has exactly one.

**Consequence:** the integration test file is in coverage `omit`, since it is
collected but deselected in the default suite. The larger runtime integration of
FastStream inside the Litestar app is explicitly out of scope.

testing-strategy.md#coverage-exclusions-.text:
Reachable error handling (web 503s, CLI exit codes, GUI/TUI "unknown"
degradation, MCP error text) is unit-tested. Only irreducible blocking calls
and the `__main__` dispatchers carry a per-site `# pragma: no cover`. The
`omit` globs are `*/`-anchored (`*/_version.py`, `*/worker/test_integration.py`,
the latter directory-anchored), and `[tool.coverage.paths]` maps
`*/site-packages/<pkg>` back onto `src/<pkg>`.

**Reason:** testing the worker exposed that *no* optional-component project
reached the 99% gate out of the box, because entrypoints and fallbacks were
unexercised and the example input disabled every component. An earlier
iteration excluded them with blanket `exclude_lines` regexes (`def main(`,
`except PackageNotFoundError`); a regex matching a `def` line excludes the
whole function body, which silently un-measured the *tested* GUI/TUI
entrypoints and web handlers — the gate became blind to what it protects. Two
further defects were universal: a `src/**`-anchored omit missed the installed
copy and reported `_version.py` at 0%, and a paths mapping that never matched
tox's per-env `site-packages` kept a separate copy per interpreter so a
version-gated line covered in one counted as missed. Both are invisible under
editable `pytest` and appear only under a real multi-env `tox run`.

**Rejected alternative:** blanket `exclude_lines` regexes — the blindness above.

**Consequence:** coverage is verified only via the installed-package `tox run`
path; after the fix every component and the base project report 100%.

testing-strategy.md#interactive-componen.text:
Each component isolates its blocking call (Textual `App.run`, the Tk dialog,
`uvicorn.run`, the MCP stdio transport and loop, the FastStream loop) in a
private helper, and the public orchestration function takes a keyword-only
driver or runner defaulting to it. Tests drive the TUI with Textual's headless
pilot, the GUI with a tracking driver and a stubbed `tkinter` module (so its
default driver carries no pragma at all), the web runner with a stub asserting
the dev-mode loopback override, the MCP transport and runner, and the worker's
lifecycle hooks by their log records. CLI subcommand bodies are tested by
monkeypatching the target component's `main`, importing the submodule
explicitly because package `__init__` re-exports shadow it. The web seam is a
`Protocol` because `reload` is keyword-only and ruff's boolean-trap rules are
on.

**Reason:** the entrypoints previously carried broad `# pragma: no cover` over
setup, widget composition, bind resolution, error handling and dispatch glue,
so a regression there slipped through and the line between irreducible and
testable was blurred. A seam is one default argument and one call — no
registry, no runtime cost — and does not cross component boundaries.

**Rejected alternative:** monkeypatching the private default helper — Python
binds a default argument at definition time, so patching the module attribute
silently no-ops; the driver must be passed. Monkeypatching stays correct for
the CLI dispatchers, which look their target up at call time.

**Consequence:** two deliberate behaviour changes: the TUI imports `textual` at
module scope, so a missing Textual raises on import instead of degrading to
stdout (a hard dependency being absent is a broken install), and the GUI
catches `Exception` around an injected driver while keeping its specific
"Tkinter not available" arm first.

testing-strategy.md#async-testing-is-an-.text:
`async_style` offers `none`, `asyncio` and `anyio`; it defaults to `none` for a
synchronous project and to `asyncio` when an async-capable component is
selected. `asyncio` adds pytest-asyncio in strict mode (every async test
explicitly marked); `anyio` adds `anyio[trio]` with a fixture parametrized over
both backends. A project rendering TUI, MCP or worker tests cannot pick `none`.
Tests for asyncio-native integrations (FastStream workers, Textual's pilot)
select asyncio explicitly.

**Reason:** a synchronous library should not gain an async runner merely because
it came from this template, while async projects need one that works
immediately; AnyIO may expose backend assumptions an asyncio-only suite would
not, so component tests that require asyncio constrain that locally.

**Rejected alternative:** always ship pytest-asyncio — the dependency on a
synchronous library; alternatives beyond this are not recorded.
